exercises.prompt:
What is `length(cfg)`?

```r
cfg <- list(title = "Survey", waves = c(2024, 2026),
            owner = list(name = "Ife", team = "stats"))
```

feedback.message: Not yet. length() counts the top-level elements only; the vector and the nested list each count as one element.

hints: Count the names at the top level of the list() call.
exercises.solution: The list has three top-level elements, `title`, `waves` and `owner`, so its length is **3**. The nested list `owner` has its own length, 2.

exercises.prompt: With `cfg` as in the previous exercise, which expression returns the number `2026`?

options.label: `cfg[["waves"]][2]`
options.feedback: Yes. [[ takes the vector out of the list, and [2] picks its second element.

options.label: `cfg["waves"][2]`
options.feedback: Not yet. cfg["waves"] is a list of length one, so its second element does not exist; the result is a list containing NULL.

options.label: `cfg[2][2]`
options.feedback: Not yet. Single brackets keep returning lists; you never reach the numbers.

options.label: `cfg$waves[[2024]]`
options.feedback: Not yet. [[2024]] asks for the 2024th element, which does not exist.

hints: Which operator returns the element itself rather than a smaller list?
exercises.solution: `cfg[["waves"]]` (or `cfg$waves`) extracts the numeric vector `c(2024, 2026)`, and `[2]` takes its second element, 2026. Single brackets on a list return a list, so `cfg["waves"]` is a list containing the vector, not the vector.

exercises.prompt:
What does the last line print? Write it with single spaces.

```r
pets <- data.frame(name = c("Kito", "Luna", "Milo", "Nala"),
                   kind = c("cat", "dog", "cat", "dog"),
                   age  = c(3, 7, 1, 5))
pets[pets$age > 2, "name"]
```

feedback.message: Not yet. Kito is 3, which is greater than 2.

hints: The row part keeps the pets older than 2; the column part picks the name column.
A single column selected with [ is returned as a vector.
exercises.solution: The condition `pets$age > 2` is TRUE for Kito (3), Luna (7) and Nala (5). Selecting one column drops to a character vector: `[1] "Kito" "Luna" "Nala"`.

exercises.prompt: With the same `pets` data frame, what does `pets[order(pets$age), ][1, "name"]` print?

feedback.message: Not yet. order(pets$age) sorts the rows by age before [1, "name"] takes the first row.

hints: Sort the rows by age first, then take the first row's name.
exercises.solution: `order(pets$age)` is `3 1 4 2`, so the sorted table starts with Milo (age 1). Taking row 1's name gives `[1] "Milo"`.

exercises.prompt:
How many rows does the **left** join have?

```r
a <- data.frame(id = c(1, 2, 3, 4), city = c("Kumasi", "Lyon", "Medan", "Natal"))
b <- data.frame(id = c(2, 4, 4, 5), visits = c(10, 3, 8, 1))
nrow(merge(a, b, by = "id", all.x = TRUE))
```

feedback.message: Not yet. id 4 appears twice in b, so Natal matches two rows and appears twice.
That is the inner join (2 once, 4 twice). all.x = TRUE also keeps ids 1 and 3 from a, with NA visits.

hints: Count the matches for each id in a: 1, 2, 3 and 4.
Unmatched rows of a are kept once each; id 5 in b is not kept.
exercises.solution: id 1: no match, kept once with NA. id 2: one match. id 3: no match, kept once. id 4: two matches, so two rows. Total **5**. The inner join would have 3 rows. Duplicate keys multiply rows, so check counts after every merge.

exercises.prompt: A function receives a data frame `df` and a character vector `cols` of column names chosen by the caller, and runs `x <- df[, cols]` followed by `nrow(x)`. It works in testing but fails when a user passes a single column name. Why, and what is the fix?

options.label: With one column, [ drops the result to a vector, whose nrow() is NULL; write df[, cols, drop = FALSE].
options.feedback: Yes. drop = FALSE keeps the result a data frame whatever the number of columns.

options.label: Data frames cannot be indexed by a single name; use df$cols instead.
options.feedback: Not yet. df$cols looks for a column literally named "cols".

options.label: cols must be a list, not a character vector.
options.feedback: Not yet. A character vector of names is the normal way to select columns.

options.label: nrow() only works on matrices.
options.feedback: Not yet. nrow() works on data frames; the problem is that x is no longer one.

hints: What type of object does crops[1:2, "farm"] return in the lesson?
exercises.solution: Selecting a single column with `[` simplifies the result to a plain vector, and `nrow()` of a vector is `NULL`. Writing `df[, cols, drop = FALSE]` always returns a data frame. (Tibbles never drop, which avoids the problem.)

exercises.prompt: A file has one row per student and columns `maths_2025`, `maths_2026`, `art_2025`, `art_2026` holding marks. In tidy form, what should one row be?

options.label: One mark: a student, a subject, a year and the mark.
options.feedback: Yes. The variables are student, subject, year and mark; each observation (one mark) becomes a row.

options.label: One student, as now.
options.feedback: Not yet. Subject and year are variables hidden in the column names, which makes grouping by them awkward.

options.label: One subject, with a column per student.
options.feedback: Not yet. That is another wide layout; students would become column names.

options.label: One year, with all marks for that year in a list column.
options.feedback: Not yet. That hides the observations inside cells rather than giving each its own row.

hints: What are the variables? Some of them are hiding in the column names.
exercises.solution: The column names encode two variables, subject and year. Tidy data has one row per observation, here one mark, with columns `student`, `subject`, `year` and `mark`. Then "average mark per subject per year" is a simple grouped mean.
